newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Global air liberalisation said to help boost jobs.
newsitem.headline: Global air liberalisation said to help boost jobs.

text.p: Liberalisation of global air transport would help the travel and tourism sector, already the world's largest industry, create millions of new jobs, an international industry group said on Wednesday.

"Freer trade in the air will speed the growth of travel and tourism and make an important contribution to economic growth and employment," the World Travel and Tourism Council (WTTC) said in a report entitled Air Transport and Freer World Trade.

But it acknowledged that a global deal to liberalise aviation seemed "unlikely for many years". It listed alternative ways forward, including agreements within and between regions as well as bilateral agreements.

"Aviation liberalisation within regions is advancing, particularly where broader free trade arrangements are in place. One of the best hopes for future strategy is to build on this momentum," the report said.
The lobby group said the travel and tourism industry generates directly or indirectly more than 10 percent of global jobs, gross domestic product and investment.

"With enlightened policies we anticipate more than 40 percent growth in this economic contribution in real terms by 2007," the report said. "A free-flowing, competitive air transport system is fundamental to this development. It will fuel markets through price competition and service innovation."
The WTTC represents more than 80 chief executive officers from all sectors of the travel and tourism industry, including airlines such as British Airways and American Airlines.
The report on air liberalisation will be presented at a travel and tourism world summit to be held in Vilamoura in the Algarve in southern Portugal on January 17-19.

WTTC president Geoffrey Lipman told a news conference many other sectors had been liberalised as a result of international trade agreements, such as the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade and the North American Free Trade Agreement.
"Aviation, which should be the first item on all of these agendas, is usually the one that gets left off because the traditional vested interests say aviation is special," he said.
The report stressed the need for effective market access, the rolling back of restrictions on establishment and ownership, harmonised competition rules, and the elimination of state aids.

Within regions, the 15-nation EU completes deregulation of its market this year and the United States and Canada, which both deregulated their domestic markets earlier, have reached a deal which goes a long way toward a single aviation market.
Such regions could then strike deals with each other.

"The most important agreement of this kind, likely to be considered in the medium term, would be between the European Union, the United States and Canada," the report said, adding that such a market would cover 60 percent of world air traffic.

Last year, the European Commission was given a mandate to start talks with the United States on establishing a Common Aviation Area. The United States already has bilateral "open skies" agreements with 10 EU countries.
